newsitem.title: GERMANY: German anti-nuclear activists attack buildings.
newsitem.headline: German anti-nuclear activists attack buildings.

text.p: Suspected anti-nuclear activists smashed windows in the northern city of Hamburg as tension mounted on Tuesday ahead of the latest controversial shipment of atomic waste to a north German nuclear dump.

Greenpeace activists in France said part of the consignment had left a reprocessing plant near the port of Cherbourg, and leaders of Germany's environmentalist Greens said they planned to join mass protests when the containers reached the dump.

The medium-term nuclear storage site at Gorleben, east of Hanover, is a favourite target of the anti-nuclear movement. Last year more than 19,000 police and border guards joined the biggest security operation in German peacetime history to overcome protesters and get a shipment to the plant.

Hamburg police said protesters damaged an electricity works building, a bank and a German railways building overnight, the latest in a wave of recent incidents in which campaigners have also sawn up rail tracks and sabotaged a high-speed train line.
They said they had found leaflets criticising the transport of nuclear waste at all three sites.

Greens spokesman Juergen Trittin accused the Bonn government of trying to overcome protests by force for political gain, and said there was no reason why the material could not be stored at nuclear power stations for now.
"You only need to resort to police state methods if you produce nuclear waste every day and have no concept for how to dispose of it," he told a news conference.
But Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of the liberal Free Democrats, junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, called Trittin's comments a "scandal".

He said Greens support for anti-nuclear demonstrators might be seen as support for the kind of violent protests and damage to property which accompanied the last shipment of waste, and urged him to renounce violence publicly.

The latest delivery of waste is likely to reach Gorleben in early March. It will include the two rail containers from France and four more from German power plants, being moved at the same time to save costs for the required security operation.

Greenpeace in Paris said two containers had left the La Hague plant near Cherbourg, but would take two weeks to reach their destination. A spokeswoman for the state reprocessing company, COGEMA, declined to comment.
